author: Dostoevsky
title: The Grand Inquisitor
where: *The Brothers Karamazov*, Part II, Book V, Chapter 5
about: Ivan Karamazov, twenty-three, sits in a tavern with his brother Alyosha, twenty and a novice in a monastery. Alyosha has just said that there is a Being who can forgive everything, and Ivan tells him a story he made up about a year ago and calls a poem. In Seville in the sixteenth century Christ comes back for a moment, and the Grand Inquisitor, a cardinal of almost ninety, has him arrested and comes alone at night to the prison. The English is Constance Garnett’s, of 1912.

view.says: Auden wrote that the evidence for Satan’s argument, when he holds out the world’s kingdoms to Jesus, is perhaps nowhere put so fully and forcefully as by the Grand Inquisitor. Jesus gives him no answer, as he gave none to Satan or to Pilate, because none is needed. Such men are answered by their own experience. They know they have failed, and that knowledge, with the hatred they have stirred up, makes them cry out.
view.quote: their own experience answers for them and they know very well what they do, and that they have failed
view.source: *The Prolific and the Devourer* (written 1939; Ecco Press, 1994), p. 51

plates.heading: The first words in the prison

lenses.label: Questions
lenses.name: hypophora
lenses.plain: a speaker asks a question and at once answers it himself
lenses.caption: The old man asks four questions here. The first, asked twice, gets no reply, and he forbids one: Don’t answer, be silent. After each of the others he goes straight on with a statement of his own. To ask and answer oneself is an old figure of argument, hypophora; one form of it asks an opponent what he can say: What canst Thou say, indeed? Of a later question Ivan tells Alyosha that the old man asks it and answers the question for Him. The old man’s reason for the silence is that the Prisoner has no right to add anything. Auden’s is that Jesus does not need to answer.
lenses.why: Dostoevsky has the old man forbid an answer and supply his own, and has Ivan say so; the old man holds that the Prisoner has no right to add anything, and Auden that he has no need to answer.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and the Russian text, which has the same questions and the same replies in the same order. *Silva Rhetoricae* under *anthypophora*, which it also calls hypophora. Ivan’s two remarks to Alyosha, [a little further on](#/read/karamazov/b05c05:12). Auden: *The Prolific and the Devourer*, p. 51.

lenses.what: Who speaks in the chapter, and inside whose speech

the Prisoner.spoken: to a dead child, before his arrest

Ivan on his plan.what: Christ says nothing in the poem

lenses.caption: Of the chapter’s 9,244 words Ivan speaks 8,343, and inside his telling the old man speaks 4,988, more than half the chapter. Auden wrote that the evidence for Satan’s argument is perhaps nowhere put so fully and forcefully as by the Grand Inquisitor. Ivan says beforehand that in his poem Christ says nothing. He gives the Prisoner two words, said to a dead child before the arrest, and in the prison none; in the Russian the two are Aramaic, as Mark’s gospel gives them. Alyosha breaks in four times; after that nobody interrupts for 4,527 words. At the first interruption Ivan tells him that the one thing that counts is for the old man to have his say.
lenses.why: Ivan gives the old man more than half the chapter and the Prisoner two words, and says the one thing that counts is for the old man to have his say; Auden finds Satan’s case perhaps nowhere more fully put.
lenses.stands: A count of the words of [the chapter](#/read/karamazov/b05c05) in the text printed here; each word is given to whoever is speaking it, by the quotation marks. Ivan’s two remarks on his plan: [before he begins](#/read/karamazov/b05c05:0) and [when Alyosha first breaks in](#/read/karamazov/b05c05:10). The Prisoner’s two words: Mark 5:41, whose Aramaic the Russian text keeps. Auden: *The Prolific and the Devourer*, p. 51.

lenses.label: Word

notes.note: From an Old English word for harming or checking, built on a root that means behind. Five times the speech speaks of the Prisoner’s coming to hinder them, the last time as the reason for burning him.

He says he does not know, and does not care to know, whether this is Christ or only a likeness of him. Two thirds of the way through the speech he asks whether he does not know to whom he is speaking.
The Russian word is the same Greek one.

lenses.caption: The old man says Thou twelve times here and Thee twice. The Russian has its ordinary familiar pronoun, which the brothers also use. Garnett gives the brothers you and keeps thou, long since a word of church and literary English, for what is said to Christ and God: 220 times in the chapter, and for no one else. So in her English the threat of burning comes in the pronoun of the chapter’s prayers. The threat names the Prisoner among the heretics, a word from the Greek for one able to choose. Later in the speech the old man complains that the Prisoner left men the fearful burden of free choice.
lenses.why: Garnett keeps thou for Christ and God alone, so in English the old man threatens the Prisoner in the pronoun of the chapter’s prayers; and the word for those he burns means, at root, one who chooses.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. A count of *Thou*, *Thee*, *Thy*, *Thine* and *Thyself* in the text printed here, and of who is spoken to each time. The Russian text for the pronoun; Merriam-Webster under *thou*; the Online Etymology Dictionary under *hinder*, *semblance*, *heretic* and *heresy*. The complaint about free choice comes [later in the speech](#/read/karamazov/b05c05:19).

plates.heading: The cry
plates.label: Two thirds of the way through the speech

lenses.label: Sentences
lenses.caption: These hundred words are eleven sentences: five questions, two commands and four statements, the last of them the secret. In the rest of the old man’s long argument a sentence averages 23 words; here, nine. The first two questions ask why, and no answer follows either. The first command is Be angry. The later questions he answers himself, and one answer is that whatever he has to tell is known to Thee already. Then he tells the secret, which nobody has asked for. The short questions are Dostoevsky’s; the two commands are sentences of their own only in Garnett’s English. Auden quotes the opening of these lines as the cry of men who know they have failed.
lenses.why: A long argument breaks into short questions and commands put to a silent listener, and the secret comes out unasked; Auden quotes the opening of these lines as the cry of men who know they have failed.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. A count of sentences in the old man’s long argument, [from the three questions to his last word](#/read/karamazov/b05c05:17), in the text printed here: a sentence ends at a period, question mark or exclamation mark followed by a capital. The Russian text for how Dostoevsky divides the same lines. Auden: *The Prolific and the Devourer*, p. 51.

lenses.label: Earlier

ties.say: The same question, almost word for word. The first time he went straight on with a statement of his own. This time another question follows.
He ordered this silence himself. Now he asks why the Prisoner looks at him silently.
Early on he remarks that the Prisoner looks at him meekly and will not even be angry. Now he asks why, and orders him to be angry. In the Russian *meekly* and *mild* are forms of one word.
At first it was the old man who knew too well what the Prisoner would say. Now it is the Prisoner who knows all that he can say.

lenses.caption: The other lines shown come from the opening of the speech, about three thousand words earlier. There the old man forbids an answer, says he knows too well what the Prisoner would say, and remarks that the Prisoner looks at him meekly and will not even be angry. Here each of these comes back turned around, and in between the Prisoner has not spoken. Auden holds that such men are answered by their own experience.
lenses.why: The old man’s opening terms come back turned around after about three thousand words in which the Prisoner has said nothing; Auden holds that such men are answered by their own experience.
lenses.stands: The marks on the two passages, both from [the same chapter](#/read/karamazov/b05c05:8). A count of the old man’s words between them in the text printed here. The Russian text, in which the same words answer each other, with Wiktionary’s Russian entry for the word behind *meekly* and *mild*. Auden: *The Prolific and the Devourer*, p. 51.

lenses.label: Mystery

notes.gloss: at first he did not know
notes.note: In his first words he said he did not know who the Prisoner was, and did not care to know. Here his question takes it as known.
The three powers, he says, hold men’s conscience captive.

The spirit who tempted Christ in the wilderness. The next sentences say that the Church has been on his side for eight centuries, and took from him the last gift Christ refused, the kingdoms of the earth.
Where Alyosha speaks of the old man’s secret, the Russian has a plainer word.

lenses.caption: The paragraph has used mystery six times before these lines. It is one of the three powers the old man names, miracle, mystery and authority, and it is what the people must follow blindly. Here it is the rulers’ own. Our mystery is what they hide: that they work with the tempter and not with Christ. The Russian word means both a mystery and a secret, and Garnett keeps mystery throughout the paragraph. After the poem Alyosha gives his own account of it: the old man has no belief in God, that’s his secret, and Ivan agrees.
lenses.why: The word that named one of the Church’s three powers over the people here names what the rulers hide, that they work with the tempter; afterward Alyosha calls the secret unbelief, and Ivan agrees.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. A count of *mystery* in [this paragraph](#/read/karamazov/b05c05:20) of the text printed here. The Russian text, with Wiktionary’s Russian entry for the word. What Alyosha and Ivan say of the secret [after the poem](#/read/karamazov/b05c05:28).

lenses.caption: The old man’s speech runs 4,977 words from its first question to its last word, the Latin Dixi, with which an orator closed a speech. He builds the speech on the three temptations in the wilderness, in Matthew’s order: bread, the pinnacle of the temple, the kingdoms of the earth. These hundred words stand between the second and the third, and their secret leads into the third: his Church, he goes on, took from the tempter the last gift the Prisoner refused. Auden names the Grand Inquisitor in his account of that temptation. The words hinder us come five times in the speech, the last time as the reason for the burning.
lenses.why: The speech follows the three temptations in order, and the secret told in these lines opens the third, the gift the Prisoner refused and the Church took; it is at the third that Auden names the Grand Inquisitor.
lenses.stands: A count of the old man’s words in the text printed here, his own and those he quotes, from [his first question](#/read/karamazov/b05c05:8) to *Dixi*. Matthew 4 and Luke 4 in the King James Bible, for the order of the temptations, and Lewis and Short’s *Latin Dictionary* under *dico*, for *Dixi*. The gift taken from the tempter: [later in the same paragraph](#/read/karamazov/b05c05:20). Auden: *The Prolific and the Devourer*, pp. 49–51.

pair.label: From the opening of the speech

lenses.label: Answer
lenses.caption: The old man wants words: he longed for Him to say something. Auden writes that Jesus gives him no answer, having no need to. What comes is a kiss, told in one sentence of eighteen words, and then five words that name it: That was all His answer. The Prisoner’s verbs are approached, kissed and went away, none of them a verb of speech. The old man, after 4,977 words, says eleven more and lets out the man he was to burn. The sentences are as short in the Russian. Asked what becomes of the old man, Ivan says: The kiss glows in his heart, and his idea stays as it was.
lenses.why: The old man wants words and gets one act, which the story calls all the answer; after 4,977 words he says eleven more, lets the Prisoner go, and keeps his idea. Auden holds that Jesus has no need to answer.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage. A count of the old man’s words in the text printed here: 4,977 in [his speech](#/read/karamazov/b05c05:8) and eleven after the kiss. His promise to burn the Prisoner closes [the speech](#/read/karamazov/b05c05:21). The Russian text, where the sentences are as short and the kiss is told in the present tense. Auden: *The Prolific and the Devourer*, p. 51.

lenses.label: Again

ties.say: Each kiss comes where words were asked for. The old man longs for the Prisoner to say something. Ivan asks Alyosha a question.
Each kiss comes out of a silence. In the Russian Alyosha also kisses him *silently*, a word Garnett leaves out.
The same act in nearly the same words. The Russian has an old poetic word for the old man’s lips and the everyday word for Ivan’s.
The old man says *go* and never come again. Ivan asks for the kiss once more and then says *go*, in the Russian the same word.
Alyosha asks whether Ivan is with the old man. Ivan says that Alyosha’s kiss comes from the Prisoner’s.

lenses.caption: When the poem is over Alyosha asks Ivan And you with him, you too? Later Ivan asks whether Alyosha will renounce him, and Alyosha does what the Prisoner did: he softly kissed him on the lips, in the Russian with the same adverb and verb. Ivan names it at once: You stole that from my poem. Alyosha’s question sets Ivan beside the old man, and Ivan’s remark on the kiss sets Alyosha beside the Prisoner. The old man shudders at the kiss and says come no more. Ivan is highly delighted, and at parting asks to be kissed once more.
lenses.why: Dostoevsky has the poem’s one listener answer Ivan with the Prisoner’s kiss, in the same words, and has Ivan say where it comes from; the old man sends the Prisoner away for good, and Ivan asks for the kiss again.
lenses.stands: The marks on the two passages: the end of the poem, and [the brothers’ talk a little later](#/read/karamazov/b05c05:48) in the same chapter. The Russian text for the words the two kisses share, with Wiktionary’s Russian entries for the adverb, the verb and the two words for lips.

lenses.label: Russian

notes.note: Garnett writes *softly* four times in the chapter: for the Prisoner’s coming, his two words to the dead child, this kiss and Alyosha’s. The Russian adverb is the same in all four, and comes four more times, where she writes *slowly*, *peacefully* and *gently*.
The Russian has an old poetic word for the mouth, and the same word names the lips from which the Prisoner was to hear the secret.
When his speech is over the old man waits for the Prisoner to answer him, and this is what comes.
Garnett has *burns* for the same Russian verb earlier, where love burns in the Prisoner’s heart as he comes among the people.

lenses.caption: Four words of the ending go back to earlier places in the chapter. The Prisoner kisses softly, as he came softly and spoke softly to the dead child. The word answer goes back to the old man’s first words, which met no answer and forbade one. Where Garnett writes aged lips Dostoevsky has ninety-year-old lips. The old man is almost ninety, and by Ivan’s account he has kept silent for ninety years. Where she writes glows Dostoevsky has burns. At the Prisoner’s coming it is love that burns in His heart; at the end, in the same Russian verb and noun, the kiss burns on the old man’s heart.
lenses.why: The ending repeats words from earlier in the chapter: those of the Prisoner’s quiet coming, the forbidden answer, the old man’s ninety years and the love burning in the Prisoner’s heart; Garnett’s English keeps two of the four.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and a count of *softly* in the text printed here. The Russian text, with Wiktionary’s Russian entries for the words behind *aged*, *lips*, *glows* and *softly*. The old man’s age and his ninety years of silence: [earlier in the chapter](#/read/karamazov/b05c05:10). The Prisoner’s [coming](#/read/karamazov/b05c05:6).

auden.says: Auden’s account of the temptations in the wilderness stands under a sentence from this chapter, signed Dostoyevsky: the old man’s remark that the three questions gather up the whole of mankind’s later history. Auden reads them as the temptations of childhood, of adolescence and of maturity. In the third, he says, Satan appeals to reason: truth is tested by success or failure, people love only themselves, and so the true way lies in being stronger than one’s neighbor. By claiming that he can give the kingdoms, Auden adds, Satan claims to be God.
auden.source: *The Prolific and the Devourer* (written 1939; Ecco Press, 1994), pp. 48–51

auden.says: Auden then writes the answer Jesus might have made if he had been listening to an attendant who only repeated his master’s words, and not to the Inquisitor. It takes up three of the old man’s sentences in turn: that men find nothing harder to bear than freedom, that the wish to worship in common is their chief misery, and that the Church has corrected Christ’s work and rested it on miracle, mystery and authority. The freedom Jesus holds out, the answer says, is freedom to know what is true, and each person must find that by his own faith and effort.
auden.source: *The Prolific and the Devourer* (written 1939; Ecco Press, 1994), pp. 51–58

auden.says: In that answer Jesus says that the Inquisitor, and not he, has turned the Last Supper into a mystery. Later in the book Auden states what history must show if Jesus was right: a general movement toward unity and equality, which the way of love has always helped, and which the way of hatred and force has always hindered and has always failed in the end to prevent. If history does not show it, he writes, then Jesus was mistaken and the right lay with Satan and the Inquisitor.
auden.source: *The Prolific and the Devourer* (written 1939; Ecco Press, 1994), pp. 54 and 62

auden.says: Charles Miller, a student in the class who also shared Auden’s house, gives Auden’s words at the first meeting, in early October 1941, as he reconstructs them. Auden named *The Brothers Karamazov* among the great books the students would be examined on, with the *Divine Comedy*, Augustine’s *Confessions* and four plays of Shakespeare. No record has been found of what he said in class about the novel.
auden.source: Charles H. Miller, *Auden: An American Friendship* (1983), pp. 26–27

auden.says: In the spring of 1943 Auden put a chart on the table of his seminar on Romanticism at Swarthmore College. In its row for the hero it lists the Grand Inquisitor with Iago and Stavrogin under The Demonic Villain, in the column headed “Hell of the Pure Word,” knowledge without power.
auden.source: Chart of 1943, reproduced in Edward Mendelson, *Early Auden, Later Auden: A Critical Biography* (2017), pp. 554–55

caveats: Auden’s view is from *The Prolific and the Devourer*, written in 1939 and not published by him, which was read here only in search snippets of a scanned copy. No mention of the kiss was found in it, so the third passage cites him only for the Prisoner’s silence.
Nothing Auden said about the novel in the 1941 class is on record. That he named it at the first meeting comes from a student’s memoir written about forty years later.

The English is Constance Garnett’s. She sometimes cuts Dostoevsky’s sentences shorter, tells the kiss in the past tense where he uses the present, and does not always keep his repeated words (*aged* for ninety-year-old, *glows* for burns).

The counts follow the text printed here. A row of dots is not counted as a word, two words joined by a dash count as one, the quotation marks decide who speaks each word, and a sentence ends at a period, question mark or exclamation mark before a capital.
The figure in the first passage has several names. The handbook used here lists it under anthypophora and gives hypophora, the name Peacham used for it in 1577, as another.
